en.title: Health Information Management: the whole course
en.short: How the health information management course is organised, what it covers and how to study it.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text:
These notes teach concepts for students of health information management. They are not medical advice and do not replace your teachers, textbooks, national laws or official standards. They give no drug doses.

Clinical guidelines and health rules change and differ between countries, so check the current national or World Health Organization (WHO) guidance, and your own country’s law and regulator, before you act. Patient information is sensitive: use examples and datasets only as your institution and the law allow.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Health information management (HIM) is the profession that plans, collects, checks, stores, protects, uses and releases health information. It connects medicine, law, management and computing.

The core idea is the information cycle: data are recorded at care, then turned into information and knowledge for decisions. HIM professionals keep records complete and confidential, code diagnoses and procedures, run routine reports, support quality and research, and help design safe electronic systems. They work in hospitals, clinics, public health agencies, insurers, ministries and technology teams.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Awards and length differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, students may take a BSc in Health Information Management or a polytechnic Higher National Diploma in health information management; registration is through the Health Records Officers Registration Board of Nigeria.

In the United States, the registered health information administrator (RHIA) credential from the American Health Information Management Association (AHIMA) is common. In the United Kingdom, many roles sit within health informatics and clinical coding. Programmes usually begin with foundations, then core HIM, then a project or master’s. Some include supervised practice.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics build the base: the profession and information cycle; medical terminology; anatomy and physiology for HIM; health care systems; health records management; computer literacy and office applications; foundations of health statistics; health data, information and knowledge; and communication, documentation and professional conduct.

Core topics apply that base: clinical coding and classification; electronic health records; health information systems and routine reporting; health data standards and interoperability; biostatistics; epidemiology and surveillance; data quality and integrity; privacy, confidentiality and security; health law and ethics; release of information and patient access; quality improvement and patient safety; HIM operations and leadership; health financing, billing and reimbursement; public health informatics and registries; and research methods.

Master’s topics go further: advanced health informatics; health data analytics and predictive modelling; advanced research methods and a dissertation; and data governance, artificial intelligence and ethics. Teaching order can vary, but the logic is usually from records and data to systems, law, management and analysis.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn the information cycle as a chain: collect, check, store, use, share, protect and dispose. For every topic ask what data are involved, who owns them, what law applies and what decision the information supports. Practise with sample records, coding exercises and small datasets, but remove names and identifiers first.

Use official classifications and standards only in their current edition. Test yourself with short cases and calculations, and keep a glossary of terms. Link each rule to its country and source. Work in groups to discuss confidentiality cases, but never share real patient data.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often memorise definitions without the workflow, so they cannot say who does what. Some quote one country’s law or one coding rule as universal.

Others treat data quality as only completeness, when accuracy, timeliness, consistency and validity also matter. A serious mistake is discussing identifiable patients outside approved settings. Another is copying figures or standards without checking the edition or source. In assignments, cite official guidance and say which country it applies to.

keyPoints: HIM manages health information across its cycle, from collection to safe release.
The course moves from foundations and records to coding, systems, law, quality, leadership and analysis.
Awards, registration and degree length differ by country, so check your own handbook and regulator.
Learn each rule with its country, current edition and official source.
Protect patient confidentiality in every exercise and use de-identified data.
These notes teach concepts and are not medical advice or a substitute for official guidance.

en.title: Health information management: the profession and the information cycle
en.short: What HIM is, how health data become useful information, and who works in the field.

sections.heading: What HIM is
sections.text: Health information management (HIM) is the profession that plans, collects, checks, stores, protects and uses health information. It supports safe care, administration and public health. HIM combines health knowledge, management, information technology, law and ethics. HIM professionals work in hospitals, clinics, public health agencies, insurers, research teams and system suppliers. Job titles and regulation vary by country: some countries require registration with a national board, while others rely on professional certification. Professional bodies include the American Health Information Management Association (AHIMA) and the International Federation of Health Information Management Associations (IFHIMA). In Nigeria, the Health Records Officers Registration Board of Nigeria is a national example. Check your country’s rules.

sections.heading: The information cycle
sections.text: Health data move through a cycle. Data capture records facts at the point of care: registration details, history, diagnosis, tests and treatment. Validation checks completeness, accuracy and patient identity. Storage and retrieval keep records safe and available to authorised users. Processing turns data into information through coding (assigning standard codes such as ICD to diagnoses), classification, counting and analysis. Dissemination shares results with those who need them. Use applies information in care, administration and public health. Feedback then improves capture. A missing diagnosis code weakens a monthly report, so the records officer checks the source record and corrects the entry.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: At a district clinic in Ghana, a patient named Ama is registered. The records officer captures her age, sex, diagnosis and treatment, checks that the diagnosis is present, stores the record securely and sends a weekly tally to the district team. The tally helps order medicines and shows a rise in malaria cases. If her record is incomplete, the clinic may plan poorly.

sections.heading: Roles and careers
sections.text: Roles include records capture, coding, data quality, release of information, systems support, analytics and management. Settings include hospitals, clinics, public health agencies, insurers, research and government. Careers progress from assistant or technician to officer, manager and director, with further study in informatics or analytics. Requirements differ by country, so check local registration and employer rules.

keyPoints: HIM is the profession that manages health information across its whole cycle.
The cycle runs from data capture through validation, storage, processing, dissemination and use.
Complete and accurate capture is essential because later reports and decisions depend on it.
HIM supports direct care, administration and public health.
Roles include records, coding, data quality, release of information, systems, analytics and management.
Titles, registration and professional bodies vary by country; check local rules.

en.title: Medical terminology for health records
en.short: Word roots, prefixes, suffixes, combining forms and common record abbreviations, with reading and checking examples.

sections.heading: Building blocks
sections.text: Medical terms are built from a word root, the main meaning, plus a prefix before it and a suffix after it. A combining form is the root with a vowel, usually o, added to join parts, as in cardi/o. Read the suffix first, then the root, then the prefix. For example, gastr/o means stomach and -itis means inflammation, so gastritis is inflammation of the stomach. Brady- means slow, tachy- fast, hyper- high, hypo- low and dys- difficult or abnormal. Hepat/o (liver) plus -megaly (enlargement) gives hepatomegaly, enlargement of the liver.

sections.heading: Systems and disease
sections.text: Body system terms often combine a root with -logy (study of), -pathy (disease) or -itis (inflammation). Cardi/o means heart, so cardiology is the study of the heart. Nephr/o means kidney, so nephritis is inflammation of the kidney. Disease terms may describe a finding: haem/o means blood and -uria means urine condition, so haematuria is blood in the urine. Cyan/o means blue and -osis means condition, so cyanosis is a bluish discolouration of the skin. Check spelling in a medical dictionary; similar roots look alike.

sections.heading: Investigations and procedures
sections.text: Investigation terms end in -gram (record or image), -graphy (recording) or -scopy (viewing). A chest X-ray is abbreviated CXR, and an electrocardiogram is ECG. Procedure suffixes include -ectomy (removal), -otomy (incision) and -plasty (repair). Colon/o means colon, so colonoscopy is viewing the colon, and appendicectomy is removal of the appendix. Abbreviations such as BP (blood pressure), HR (heart rate), Hb (haemoglobin) and WBC (white blood cell count) are common, but they vary by country and hospital. Use the approved local list and write the full term if in doubt.

sections.heading: Checking a record
sections.text: At a clinic in Kano, records clerk Amina sees 'CXR: RLL pneumonia'. She reads CXR as chest X-ray, RLL as right lower lobe and pneumonia as a disease term. She checks the clinic abbreviation list and asks the clinician if an abbreviation is not listed. She does not guess or alter the entry. This protects data quality and patient safety.

keyPoints: Read a medical term from the suffix, then the root, then the prefix.
A combining form is a root plus a vowel, usually o, used to join word parts.
Common suffixes include -itis for inflammation and -ectomy for removal.
Investigation terms often use -gram, -graphy and -scopy; procedures use -ectomy, -otomy and -plasty.
Abbreviations vary by country and hospital, so use the approved local list.
Check unclear terms in a dictionary or with the clinician; never guess in the record.

en.title: Anatomy and physiology for health information work
en.short: Body systems, disease and procedure terms, and why anatomy supports accurate records and coding.

sections.heading: Systems and terms
sections.text: Anatomy is structure; physiology is function. Health information staff need an overview of the major systems: cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, nervous, musculoskeletal, endocrine, urinary, reproductive, immune and skin. Each has organs and normal functions. Records use terms such as myocardial infarction (heart muscle damage from blocked blood supply), pneumonia (lung infection), gastritis (stomach inflammation), diabetes mellitus (raised blood glucose from insulin problems), urinary tract infection and fracture. Knowing the organ and process helps read a record correctly.

sections.heading: Disease and procedure terms
sections.text: Disease terms often combine a body part, process and cause: nephritis is kidney inflammation; hepatitis is liver inflammation; osteoarthritis is joint disease with cartilage breakdown. Procedure terms name an operation or test: appendectomy is removal of the appendix; cholecystectomy is removal of the gallbladder; arthroscopy is looking inside a joint; hysterectomy is removal of the uterus; caesarean section is birth by abdominal surgery. Prefixes and suffixes help, but confirm in a standard dictionary rather than guessing.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Accurate documentation depends on precise anatomy. Right hip replacement and right hip arthroscopy are different procedures and may classify differently. A coder or records officer who knows the body system can spot missing details, such as site, laterality (left or right) and procedure type, and query the clinician. This supports classification and statistics. It does not make the health information worker a diagnostician or clinician; diagnosis and treatment remain clinical duties.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: A record for Amina says fracture, left femur, treated by internal fixation. The worker recognises femur as thigh bone and fixation as surgical stabilisation. If the site or side were missing, the record would be incomplete for coding and reporting. The worker asks the clinician to clarify, without deciding the diagnosis.

keyPoints: Anatomy is structure; physiology is function.
Major body systems include cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, nervous, musculoskeletal, endocrine, urinary, reproductive, immune and skin.
Disease terms usually name a body part, process or cause; procedure terms name an operation or test.
Precise anatomy, including site and laterality, is needed for accurate records and classification.
Health information workers may query missing details but do not diagnose or treat.
Use a standard medical dictionary when a term is unclear.

en.title: Health care systems and organisations
en.short: Levels of care, public and private providers, patient and record flow, and how systems differ.

sections.heading: Levels and providers
sections.text: A health system includes all organisations, people and resources whose main aim is to promote, restore or maintain health. Health systems organise care in levels. Primary care is the first point of contact: general clinics, community health workers and family doctors. It handles common problems, prevention and referral. Secondary care is specialist care, usually in hospitals, received after referral. Tertiary care is advanced or rare specialist care, such as cardiac surgery or cancer centres. Some systems also speak of quaternary care for highly specialised services. Providers may be public (government owned), private for-profit, or private not-for-profit and faith-based. Many people also use pharmacies and traditional healers.

sections.heading: Patient and record flow
sections.text: Patients usually enter at primary care and move upward by referral, then return with a discharge summary. Records should follow the same path. A unique patient identifier, a referral letter and a discharge summary link the levels. Case: Amina attends a primary health centre with fever. The clinic records her history and refers her to a district hospital. If both use the same identifier and share a summary, the hospital sees her earlier results and the clinic receives follow-up instructions. If not, staff repeat tests and create duplicate records.

sections.heading: Organisation and financing
sections.text: Countries differ in organisation, financing and regulation, and this shapes health information work. Organisation may be centralised or decentralised. Financing may come from taxes, social health insurance, private insurance, out-of-pocket payments or donors. Regulation sets licensing, privacy, reporting and coding rules. For example, the United Kingdom has a mainly tax-funded public system; Germany uses statutory health insurance; the United States relies heavily on private insurance, with public programmes too. In low-income settings, out-of-pocket payment and donor reporting are common. These differences affect what data are collected, who may see them, how records are coded for payment, and which reports are mandatory. Always check current national law and guidance.

keyPoints: Primary care is first contact; secondary and tertiary care are specialist levels reached mainly by referral.
Providers can be public, private for-profit or private not-for-profit, and patients may also use pharmacies and traditional healers.
Records should follow the patient through a unique identifier, referral letter and discharge summary.
Countries differ in organisation, financing and regulation, so data collection, access, coding and reporting rules vary.
Financing models include taxes, social health insurance, private insurance, out-of-pocket payments and donors.
Health information staff must follow current national law and reporting guidance, not assume one country’s rules apply everywhere.

en.title: Health records management
en.short: Patient record content, forms, identification, numbering, MPI, filing, tracking, retention and hybrid records.

sections.heading: Record content
sections.text: A patient health record is the organised information about one person’s care. It usually has identification data, clinical notes, orders, results, consent forms and correspondence. Good records are complete, accurate, legible, dated and authenticated. Structure follows the care process: registration, history, examination, investigations, treatment and discharge. Each entry should identify the author and time. A record is a legal document, so errors are corrected by a single line through the entry with date and initials, or a dated addendum for late information; never erase.

sections.heading: Forms and identity
sections.text: Forms design controls data quality. A form should collect only needed data, use clear labels and standard terms, allow enough space, and place identifiers on every page. Patient identification needs at least two identifiers, such as full name plus date of birth or a unique hospital number. Names alone are unsafe because spelling and common names cause duplicates. Case: Amina Bello registers twice as Amina Belo and Amina Bello; staff use the master patient index to link the records to one identifier.

sections.heading: Numbering and MPI
sections.text: A numbering system gives each patient a unique number. In a unit system, one number follows the person across all visits. In a serial system, each visit gets a new number. A serial-unit system gives a new number each visit but files all records under the first number. The master patient index (MPI) is the list or database of all patients with their identifiers and record numbers. It is the key to finding and linking records and preventing duplicates. Search the MPI before creating a new record.

sections.heading: Filing and retention
sections.text: Paper records are filed by alphabetic, numeric or terminal digit order; numeric systems are common. Tracking records means recording every movement, often with a sign-out card or tracer, so records can be found. Retention is how long records are kept; periods vary by country, facility and record type, so check current national law or ministry guidance. Disposal must be authorised, documented and secure, by shredding or incineration. Hybrid records mix paper and electronic files. They need one identifier, clear rules on which part is official, and reconciliation when paper is scanned.

keyPoints: A patient health record is a legal document; correct errors with a dated, signed correction or addendum, never erasure.
Use at least two patient identifiers and search the master patient index before creating a new record.
Forms should collect only needed data and carry patient identifiers on every page.
Numbering systems include unit, serial and serial-unit; the MPI links all identifiers and records.
Track every record movement and follow the current national retention and disposal rules, which vary by country.
Hybrid records need one identifier, clear rules on the official record, and reconciliation after scanning.

en.title: Computer literacy and office applications for health information
en.short: Hardware, software, files, safe email and internet, plus spreadsheets and databases for health data.

sections.heading: Hardware and software
sections.text: Hardware is the physical equipment: computers, screens, keyboards, printers and drives. Software is the set of instructions that makes hardware work. An operating system (OS) is the main software that manages memory, files, devices and user accounts; examples are Windows, macOS and Linux. Application software does a task, such as a word processor, spreadsheet or database. Use systems approved by your organisation and keep them updated.

sections.heading: Files and safe use
sections.text: A file is a named store of data, such as a document or image. A folder groups files. Use clear names, avoid personal identifiers in file names, and save in approved locations. Email and internet use carry risks. Check the sender, be careful with links and attachments, and never share passwords. Use strong, unique passwords, lock your screen, and log out. Phishing is a message that tricks you into revealing information or installing harmful software. Report suspected phishing locally.

sections.heading: Spreadsheets for health data
sections.text: A spreadsheet is a grid of rows and columns; each box is a cell. Cells hold numbers, text or formulas, which calculate values. Use spreadsheets for small tables, cleaning and charts. Clean data by removing duplicate rows, standardising dates and units, checking missing values and using validation rules. Stays of 3, 5, 7 and 9 days total 24 days, average 6 days. A formula such as =AVERAGE(B2:B5) calculates this. Label charts and do not hide the scale.

sections.heading: Databases and protection
sections.text: A database stores related data in tables. A table has records (rows) and fields (columns). A primary key uniquely identifies each record, such as a patient number. Databases suit larger, linked data and controlled access better than spreadsheets. Back up data regularly, keep copies in more than one secure place, and test restores. Access control limits who can view or change data; give each user only the permissions their role needs. Use individual accounts, not shared passwords, and review access when roles change.

keyPoints: An operating system manages files, devices and user accounts, while applications perform tasks.
Use clear file names, approved storage and strong unique passwords; report suspected phishing.
Clean spreadsheet data by removing duplicates, standardising formats and checking missing values.
In a spreadsheet, =AVERAGE(range) returns the mean; check the range before trusting it.
A database table has records and fields, and a primary key uniquely identifies each record.
Back up regularly, test restores, and give each user only the access their role needs.

en.title: Foundations of health statistics
en.short: Rates, ratios, proportions, tables and charts: how to measure and read health data without overstating.

sections.heading: Ratios and rates
sections.text: A ratio compares two quantities, written a:b or a/b. A proportion is a ratio where the numerator is part of the denominator, so it lies between 0 and 1. A percentage is a proportion × 100. A rate measures events per population per time; it needs a numerator, a denominator of people at risk, and a period. Example: a ward has 50 patients and 5 have pressure injuries. Proportion = 5 ÷ 50 = 0.10 = 10%. Ratio of injured to not injured = 5:45 = 1:9. Always state the denominator and period.

sections.heading: Crude and specific rates
sections.text: Crude rates use the whole population. Crude death rate = deaths in a year ÷ total population × 1,000. A town of 50,000 records 400 deaths, so 400 ÷ 50,000 × 1,000 = 8 per 1,000 per year. Specific rates use a subgroup, such as age, cause or hospital service. Hospital bed occupancy rate = inpatient days ÷ available bed days × 100. A 200-bed hospital has 200 × 30 = 6,000 bed days in a 30-day month. If patients used 4,800 days, occupancy = 4,800 ÷ 6,000 × 100 = 80%. Crude rates depend on age structure, so compare specific rates when populations differ. Vital statistics include births, deaths and marriages.

sections.heading: Tables and charts
sections.text: Tabulation arranges data in rows and columns with a clear title, units and totals. Keep categories few. Bar charts compare categories, line charts show trends over time, pie charts show parts of a whole (only a few slices), and histograms show continuous distributions. Label axes, give units and name the source. Interpret cautiously. More cases may mean better reporting, not more disease. One hospital’s chart does not represent a country. Small numbers give unstable rates. Rates allow fair comparison between groups of different sizes, but they do not prove cause. Ask who was counted, who was missed, and what the denominator was.

keyPoints: Ratio compares two quantities; proportion is part over whole; percentage = proportion × 100.
Rate = events ÷ population at risk × multiplier, over a stated period.
Crude death rate = deaths ÷ total population × 1,000 per year.
Bed occupancy rate = inpatient days ÷ available bed days × 100.
Specific rates compare subgroups and are fairer when populations differ in age or case mix.
Tables and charts need titles, units and denominators; association does not prove cause.

en.title: Health data, information and knowledge
en.short: Data, information and knowledge in health care: sources, users, identifiers, tools and data quality.

sections.heading: Data to knowledge
sections.text: Data are raw facts or symbols without context: a number, word, code or image. Information is data processed, organised and interpreted so they have meaning. Knowledge is the understanding and experience that let people use information to judge and act. For example, “12” is data. “Clinic A recorded 12 new malaria cases in June” is information. “Cases rise after rains, so order tests before the rainy season” is knowledge for planning. The boundary depends on the user.

sections.heading: Sources and users
sections.text: Health data come from clinical, administrative and public health settings. Clinical sources include patient records, laboratory results, imaging reports and ward registers. Administrative sources include registration, appointments, billing and staffing records. Public health sources include surveillance, registries, surveys and vital registration of births and deaths. Users include clinicians and nurses; health information staff; administrators and finance officers; public health workers and planners; researchers; policymakers; and patients. Each needs different detail and timeliness. A clinician may need one result now; a district planner needs monthly counts.

sections.heading: Identifiers and tools
sections.text: An identifier is a code that distinguishes one person, place or event from another. A patient identifier, such as a hospital record number, links data to the right patient. Names and birth dates are unreliable alone; use a unique number and check it. Data collection tools capture data: paper registers, structured forms, questionnaires, interviews, observation, and laboratory or device systems. A good tool has clear questions, defined options, and fields for identifier, date and collector. Poor tools produce missing or inconsistent data.

sections.heading: Data quality
sections.text: Data quality has common dimensions. Accuracy means data are correct. Completeness means required fields are filled. Timeliness means data are available when needed. Consistency means the same fact is recorded the same way across forms and systems. Validity means data follow agreed rules and formats. Uniqueness means each person or event is counted once. These are introduced here and examined later. Complete but wrong data are still poor.

keyPoints: Data are raw facts without context; information is interpreted data; knowledge is understanding used to act.
Clinical, administrative and public health settings each supply different health data and have different users.
Use a unique patient identifier, not a name alone, to link data to the right person.
Data collection tools include registers, forms, questionnaires, interviews, observation and device systems.
Common data quality dimensions are accuracy, completeness, timeliness, consistency, validity and uniqueness.
Data quality matters because complete but wrong data can still mislead decisions.

en.title: Communication, documentation and professional conduct
en.short: Clear communication, correct patient identification, safe records and professional conduct in health information work.

sections.heading: Clear communication
sections.text: Communication is the exchange of information so that both people understand. Use plain language, short sentences and common words. Explain technical terms the first time you use them. Check understanding with teach-back: ask the person to say in their own words what they understood. Use a trained interpreter when needed, not a child. For colleagues, be specific and respectful. SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is a common handover structure. For the public, avoid identifying details and state the limits of the information.

sections.heading: Identification and records
sections.text:
Identify every patient before you file, retrieve or discuss a record. Use at least two identifiers, such as full name and date of birth or hospital number, as local policy requires. Never use a bed or room number as an identifier. Documentation standards require records that are accurate, complete, timely, legible and signed or authenticated. Write facts, not opinions. Use only approved abbreviations. Correct an error with a single line, then date, initial and explain; never overwrite or backdate. In electronic systems, use your own login and never share passwords.

Case: At a clinic in Ibadan, records clerk Tunde cannot find a file. He asks the patient for full name and date of birth, checks the hospital number, and searches again. He does not guess or create a duplicate file. He writes a brief note and tells his supervisor.

sections.heading: Teamwork and confidentiality
sections.text: Teamwork means knowing your role, asking for help early and handing over clearly. Respect patients and colleagues: address people by their preferred name, protect dignity and avoid gossip. Confidentiality means sharing health information only with people who need it for care or lawful work, and only the minimum necessary. Discuss cases in private, lock paper records and log out of computers. If you see a breach, report it through the proper channel. Professional conduct includes honesty, punctuality, competence and clear boundaries. Never falsify a record or hide an error; declare it and follow local policy.

keyPoints: Use plain language and teach-back to confirm that a patient understands.
Identify patients with at least two identifiers, never a bed or room number.
Document accurately, promptly and legibly, and correct errors without overwriting.
Share confidential information only on a need-to-know basis and in private.
Work as a team: know your role, hand over clearly and escalate concerns early.
Professional conduct means honesty, respect, competence and reporting errors.

en.title: Clinical coding and classification
en.short: How clinical records become standard diagnosis and procedure codes, from review to audit.

sections.heading: Why classify
sections.text: A clinical classification groups similar diseases or procedures into categories under agreed rules. A code is the label for one category. Coding turns words in the health record into these labels. This makes data comparable across patients, wards, hospitals and countries. Coded data support statistics, public health, planning, quality review, research and payment. Without them, pneumonia in one hospital cannot be counted with pneumonia in another.

sections.heading: Coding process
sections.text: The coder reviews the record: admission note, progress notes, operation note, discharge summary and results. The coder identifies the principal diagnosis, the condition chiefly responsible for admission, plus secondary diagnoses and procedures. Then the coder assigns codes using the current code book or tool and follows its rules. If documentation is unclear or contradictory, the coder queries the clinician rather than guessing. Codes are checked and entered into the health information system. Example: Amina is admitted with pneumonia and type 2 diabetes. The record supports pneumonia as principal diagnosis and diabetes as secondary. The coder assigns codes from the ICD version used locally for both, and a procedure code if one was done.

sections.heading: WHO classifications
sections.text: WHO maintains the International Classification of Diseases (ICD), the reference for diagnoses, causes of death and health problems. ICD-11 is the current version, but countries adopt versions at different times and may use national clinical modifications. WHO also publishes the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and the International Classification of Health Interventions (ICHI), a reference for procedures. Many countries use their own procedure classification or a national adaptation. Payment rules, such as diagnosis-related groups (groups of cases with similar expected costs used to set hospital payment), also differ by country and insurer, so coders must follow local rules.

sections.heading: Audit
sections.text: A coding audit compares assigned codes with the record. An auditor samples records, re-codes them independently, measures agreement and gives feedback and training. Audit finds documentation gaps, rule errors and upcoding, which is assigning a more severe code than the record supports. Regular audit protects data quality and fair payment.

keyPoints: Clinical coding converts documented diagnoses and procedures into standard codes for comparison, statistics and payment.
The coder reviews the record, identifies principal and secondary diagnoses and procedures, assigns codes by current rules, and queries unclear documentation.
WHO ICD is the reference for diagnoses; ICF covers functioning and ICHI is a reference for interventions.
Versions, national clinical modifications, procedure classifications and payment rules differ by country, so use the current local rules.
Coding audit re-codes a sample against the record to find documentation gaps, rule errors and upcoding.
Never guess a code; query the clinician and record the answer.

en.title: Electronic health records
en.short: Compare paper, hybrid and electronic records, EHR functions, implementation, downtime, legal status and risks.

sections.heading: Record types
sections.text: A health record is the documented account of a patient’s care. A paper record is familiar and needs no power, but it exists in one place, can be illegible, and cannot be viewed by two people at once. An electronic health record (EHR) is a digital, longitudinal record shared across care settings. It is searchable and can combine notes, results and orders. A hybrid record mixes paper and electronic parts, often during transition. Hybrid is workable but raises risks of missing pages, duplicate entries and unclear which part is authoritative.

sections.heading: Core functions
sections.text: Core EHR functions include clinical documentation, results viewing, order entry and decision support. Clinical documentation records notes, observations and assessments. Results viewing shows laboratory and imaging reports with previous values. Order entry, often called computerized provider order entry (CPOE), sends requests for tests, medicines and referrals. Clinical decision support (CDS) uses rules to warn about allergies, interactions or overdue tests. For example, when a clinician orders penicillin for a patient with a recorded penicillin allergy, CDS can display a warning before the order is signed. Alerts must be selective, because too many cause alert fatigue.

sections.heading: Implementation and roles
sections.text: Implementation needs workflow design, training, data migration and testing. A phased start, one unit or function at a time, is safer than a sudden switch for many hospitals. Roles differ. Clinicians document and order; nurses record observations and administer; pharmacists verify orders; laboratory and imaging staff post results; health information managers check record completeness and coding; IT staff maintain access and backups. Patients may view parts of their record through a portal.

sections.heading: Downtime, law and risk
sections.text: Downtime procedures keep care safe when systems fail: use paper forms, read-only backups and later reconciliation, meaning the paper entries are added to the record once the system is restored. Legal status varies by country. Usually the provider holds the record, while the patient has rights of access and correction; electronic records can be legal when authentic, complete and supported by an audit trail, a log of who viewed or changed the record and when. Risks are wrong-patient entry, copy-paste errors, alert fatigue, downtime data loss and confidentiality breaches. Check national law.

keyPoints: Paper records are familiar but single-location; EHRs are digital and shared; hybrid records mix both and need clear reconciliation.
Core EHR functions are clinical documentation, results viewing, order entry and clinical decision support.
CPOE sends orders and CDS warns about allergies, interactions or overdue tests, but excessive alerts cause fatigue.
Implementation needs workflow design, training, testing, data migration and defined user roles.
Downtime procedures use paper forms, read-only backups and later reconciliation to protect care.
Legal status and access rights vary by country; electronic records can be legal when authentic, complete and audited, and confidentiality risks remain.

en.title: Health information systems and routine reporting
en.short: Aggregate HMIS data flow, indicators, dashboards, feedback, system choice, training and management use.

sections.heading: Aggregate systems and flow
sections.text: An aggregate health management information system (HMIS) collects counts and summaries, not individual patient records. Facility staff record services in registers, then complete monthly summary forms. Data flow from facility to district to national level. At each level, staff check completeness, timeliness and consistency before sending data upward. The national level compiles reports for planning and comparison. DHIS2 is a widely used open-source platform for aggregate reporting, but countries choose different systems and forms.

sections.heading: Indicators and dashboards
sections.text: An indicator is a measure with a clear numerator, denominator and definition. For example, suppose a district expects 1,500 pregnancies and records 450 first antenatal visits. Antenatal coverage is 450 ÷ 1,500 × 100 = 30 per cent. The denominator must match the indicator definition, or the result misleads. A dashboard shows indicators by month, facility and district, helping managers spot gaps and compare trends. Feedback returns analysed reports to facilities with interpretation and agreed actions, not just tables.

sections.heading: Selecting and training
sections.text: Choose a system by workflow fit: it should follow how staff actually work and collect only needed data. Check usability, interoperability, privacy, cost, local support and ability to export data. Avoid parallel paper and digital reporting unless a transition plan exists. Training must cover definitions, forms, entry, validation and analysis, with supervision and refreshers. A system that staff cannot use will produce poor data, however advanced it is.

sections.heading: Feedback and data use
sections.text: Data use closes the loop. In a hypothetical case, Amina, a district HIM officer, sees two clinics reporting late. She visits, retrains staff and sets a monthly review meeting. Completeness improves, and the district uses the data to plan outreach. Routine review meetings should examine dashboards, agree actions, assign responsibilities and follow up. Feedback to facilities and use of data for decisions make reporting worthwhile and improve data quality over time.

keyPoints: An aggregate HMIS reports counts and summaries, not individual patient records.
Routine data flow from facility registers through district summaries to national reports, with checks at each level.
An indicator needs a clear numerator, denominator and definition; coverage = numerator ÷ denominator × 100.
Dashboards show trends and gaps, while feedback returns analysed reports with agreed actions.
Choose systems by workflow fit, minimum data, usability, interoperability, privacy, cost and support.
Training and routine data review meetings turn reporting into management decisions and better data quality.

en.title: Health data standards and interoperability
en.short: Identifiers, vocabularies, messaging standards, interoperability levels, exchange and mapping.

sections.heading: Identifiers and vocabularies
sections.text:
A standard is an agreed rule for representing or exchanging data. An identifier is a unique code for an object, such as a patient, clinician, facility or specimen. Good identifiers are unique, stable and never reused; a master patient index helps match records.

A vocabulary or terminology is a controlled set of terms with defined meanings. SNOMED CT is a clinical terminology for concepts such as diagnoses, findings and procedures. LOINC codes laboratory tests and observations. ICD is a classification for morbidity and mortality, not a full clinical terminology. Use the current national edition where one exists.

sections.heading: Messaging and interoperability
sections.text:
Messaging standards define the structure of data sent between systems. HL7 version 2 is widely used for messages; HL7 FHIR uses web resources for modern exchange. DICOM carries medical images and related information.

Interoperability means systems can exchange data and use it correctly. Technical or syntactic interoperability means the format is understood. Semantic interoperability means both sides share the same meaning, so a coded result is interpreted alike. Process interoperability means workflows and policies support the exchange. Standards alone do not create interoperability; governance, consent and data quality matter.

sections.heading: Exchange and mapping
sections.text:
Health information exchange (HIE) is the electronic sharing of patient data among organisations, within legal and consent rules. A common model is a regional or national exchange connected to hospitals and clinics.

Mapping is the practical work of linking local terms to standard concepts. Example: a clinic in Ibadan records "blood sugar" as a local test. The team maps it to the correct LOINC code for the exact specimen and method, records the mapping in a table, and tests it. If no exact concept exists, record the closest term and the reason. Review mappings when systems or standard versions change. Poor mapping causes wrong meaning, so semantic interoperability depends on careful, documented mapping.

keyPoints: Standards are agreed rules; identifiers must be unique, stable and not reused.
SNOMED CT covers clinical concepts; LOINC covers laboratory observations; DICOM covers images.
HL7 FHIR and HL7 version 2 are messaging standards; FHIR uses web resources.
Interoperability has technical, semantic and process levels; semantic means shared meaning.
Health information exchange is electronic sharing among organisations under legal and consent rules.
Mapping local terms to standard concepts must be documented, tested and maintained.

en.title: Biostatistics for health information
en.short: Sampling, probability, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, correlation and simple regression for health data.

sections.heading: Sampling and probability
sections.text: Biostatistics uses a sample, a selected subset, to describe a population. Probability is the chance of an event, from 0 to 1. Random sampling gives every member a known chance of selection and reduces bias. State how the sample was chosen and who was left out. The standard error (SE) measures how much an estimate varies between samples; for a mean, SE = s/√n, where s is the sample standard deviation and n the sample size.

sections.heading: Confidence intervals
sections.text: A confidence interval (CI) gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter. A 95% CI is estimate ± 1.96 × SE for a large sample. It does not mean a 95% chance that the true value lies in this particular interval. Example: mean systolic pressure 120 mmHg, SE 2 mmHg. 95% CI = 120 ± 1.96 × 2 = 120 ± 3.92, giving 116.08 to 123.92 mmHg. Report the estimate, CI and sample size.

sections.heading: Hypothesis tests
sections.text: A hypothesis test compares data with a null hypothesis, usually no difference or no association. The p value is the probability of results at least as extreme if the null is true. A small p value suggests evidence against the null, but it does not measure effect size. Report the effect, CI and p value. For one mean, t = (xbar − μ)/(s/√n), where xbar is the sample mean. Check assumptions and choose the test that fits the question.

sections.heading: Correlation and regression
sections.text: Correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables, from −1 to 1. Pearson r suits continuous data; Spearman rank correlation suits ranked or non-normal data. Correlation does not prove causation. Simple linear regression models one outcome from one predictor: y = a + bx, where a is the intercept and b the slope. Check scatterplots, outliers and residuals. Check software output: units, missing values and labels.

keyPoints: Random sampling gives every member a known chance of selection, and the standard error of a mean is SE = s/√n.
A 95% confidence interval is estimate ± 1.96 × SE for large samples and gives a range of plausible population values.
A p value is the probability of results at least as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis is true; it is not a measure of effect size.
For one mean, t = (xbar − μ)/(s/√n), where xbar is the sample mean; check assumptions and choose the test that fits the question.
Correlation r runs from −1 to 1 and measures linear association, not causation.
Simple linear regression is y = a + bx, where b is the slope; check software output and the data behind it.

en.title: Epidemiology and public health surveillance
en.short: Incidence, prevalence, risk, rates, comparisons, surveillance, notifiable reporting, registries and outbreak data.

sections.heading: Measuring disease
sections.text: Epidemiology studies the distribution and determinants of health events in populations. Incidence is the number of new cases in a defined population over a period. Prevalence is the number of existing cases at a point or during a period. A rate has a numerator, denominator and time unit; a proportion has no time unit. In a city of 100,000 people, 300 new cases in one year give an incidence of 300 ÷ 100,000 = 0.003, or 300 per 100,000 person-years. If 1,200 people have the condition at midyear, prevalence is 1,200 ÷ 100,000 = 0.012, or 1.2% (1,200 per 100,000). Prevalence rises when incidence rises or people live longer with the condition.

sections.heading: Risk and comparison
sections.text: Risk is the probability that a person free of a health event develops it over a stated period. Cumulative incidence measures risk. If 20 of 500 exposed people develop illness and 10 of 500 unexposed people do, the risks are 20 ÷ 500 = 4% and 10 ÷ 500 = 2%. The risk ratio is 4% ÷ 2% = 2.0, so the exposed group had twice the risk. Comparisons use risk ratios, rate ratios, odds ratios or standardised rates. Age standardisation adjusts for different age structures. Always state the population, period and case definition.

sections.heading: Surveillance systems
sections.text: Public health surveillance is the continuous, systematic collection, analysis and interpretation of health data, linked to action. Passive surveillance relies on routine reports; active surveillance seeks cases directly. Sentinel surveillance uses selected sites. Syndromic surveillance uses symptoms before diagnosis. Surveillance detects clusters and trends, guides response and evaluates control. Data quality depends on complete, timely and comparable reporting.

sections.heading: Reporting and outbreak data
sections.text: Notifiable disease reporting requires clinicians or laboratories to report listed conditions to authorities. Lists, legal duties and deadlines vary by country; check national guidance. WHO’s International Health Regulations (2005) require countries to notify WHO of events that may constitute a public health emergency of international concern. Registries collect cases over time. Outbreak data include case counts and dates; an epidemic curve plots cases by date of onset, and an attack rate is cases ÷ population at risk.

keyPoints: Incidence = new cases ÷ population at risk over a stated period.
Prevalence = existing cases ÷ population at a stated time or period.
Risk = new cases ÷ people at risk at the start; risk ratio = risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed.
Attack rate = cases ÷ population at risk during an outbreak.
Surveillance is continuous collection, analysis and use of health data for action.
Notifiable disease lists and legal duties vary by country; check current national guidance.

en.title: Data quality and integrity
en.short: Data quality dimensions, validation, audit, correction, metrics and effects on care, reporting and research.

sections.heading: Quality dimensions
sections.text: Data quality means how fit health data are for their intended use. Accuracy means values are correct and match the real event. Completeness means all required items are present. Timeliness means data are available when needed. Consistency means the same fact agrees across records and systems. Validity means values obey agreed rules, formats and allowed codes. A record can be complete but inaccurate, or accurate but late, so the dimensions are checked together. Data integrity adds that data are not altered or lost improperly across their life cycle.

sections.heading: Validation and verification
sections.text: Validation rules are automatic checks at entry. They include mandatory fields, range checks, format checks, cross-field checks and duplicate checks. For example, a discharge date cannot be earlier than an admission date. Validation stops some errors but cannot prove a value is true. Source-data verification compares the record with the original source, such as the patient, laboratory report or ward register. A clerk may verify a sample each month. Verification is stronger before data are sent to a national system, because later correction is harder.

sections.heading: Audit and correction
sections.text: An audit is a planned review of records against agreed criteria. It measures whether practice meets the standard and finds where errors arise. Error correction should fix the source record, document who changed what and why, and inform downstream users. Correcting only a report leaves the error in place. Root-cause review asks whether the cause was a missing field, unclear form, poor training or a system fault. Good correction prevents repeat errors rather than hiding them.

sections.heading: Effects and metrics
sections.text: Quality metrics include completeness rate, error rate and timeliness. If 200 records are checked and 10 lack a discharge date, completeness is 190 ÷ 200 × 100 = 95%. Poor data can hide allergies, distort counts and bias research. Check current national guidance for reporting rules.

keyPoints: Data quality has several dimensions, including accuracy, completeness, timeliness, consistency and validity.
Validation rules catch format, range, mandatory and duplicate errors at entry.
Source-data verification compares records with the original source.
Audit reviews records against agreed criteria and should lead to correction at source.
Completeness rate = records with required item ÷ records checked × 100, and error rate = records with errors ÷ records checked × 100.
Poor data can harm care, distort reports and bias research.

en.title: Privacy, confidentiality and information security
en.short: Privacy, confidentiality and the security controls that protect health information.

sections.heading: Privacy and confidentiality
sections.text: Privacy is a person’s right to control how their health information is collected, used and shared. Confidentiality is the duty of those who hold information to keep it private and disclose it only with consent or where the law permits. These are related but not the same: privacy is the wider right, confidentiality is the professional and organisational obligation. Patient rights and legal duties differ by country. For example, Nigeria’s National Health Act 2014, the UK’s Data Protection Act 2018, and South Africa’s Protection of Personal Information Act 2013, each set different requirements. Always check the current national law and your facility policy.

sections.heading: Security controls
sections.text: Security controls protect information from unauthorised access, loss and alteration. Access control gives each user only the minimum access needed for their role. Authentication proves identity, using something you know, such as a password, something you have, such as a token, or something you are, such as a fingerprint. Encryption converts readable data into ciphertext so that only holders of the key can read it; it protects data at rest and in transit. Backups are regular copies kept separately and tested by restoring them. Logs record who accessed what and when.

sections.heading: Breach response
sections.text: A breach is any unauthorised access, disclosure, loss or alteration of health information. A response plan should detect and contain the breach, assess the risk, notify according to national law and facility policy, and review what failed. Example: a clerk in an African hospital opens a phishing email (a fake message designed to trick staff) and malware encrypts the records server. Staff isolate the server, restore the latest tested backup, reset passwords, and inform the data protection officer. They check the law before notifying patients. Good security is continuous, not a single product.

keyPoints: Privacy is the right to control health information; confidentiality is the duty to protect it.
Access control limits each user to the minimum data needed for their role.
Authentication proves identity using knowledge, possession or biometrics.
Encryption protects data at rest and in transit; backups must be tested by restoring.
A breach response includes detection, containment, risk assessment, lawful notification and review.
Legal duties and patient rights differ by country, so check current national law and facility policy.

en.title: Health law and ethics for health information management
en.short: Consent, capacity, minors, deceased patients, retention, disclosure, coding ethics and data sharing.

sections.heading: Consent and capacity
sections.text:
Consent is permission given freely by a person who has information and can choose. Valid consent is voluntary, informed and specific. Capacity is the ability to understand, retain, weigh and communicate a decision. Adults are presumed to have capacity unless evidence suggests otherwise. Capacity can change with illness, and a person may refuse treatment even if the refusal harms them. Record the discussion, decision and who consented.

Minors usually need a parent or guardian, but many countries recognise mature minors for some decisions. Adolescent records may have special confidentiality rules. After death, confidentiality often continues; family access depends on law and any consent given before death. Do not assume next of kin can see the full record. Law differs by country, so check national law.

sections.heading: Retention and disclosure
sections.text:
Retention periods are the required keeping times set by national law, professional guidance and record type, not by habit. Keep records for the required period, then destroy them securely and document the destruction. Disclosure means sharing the record. It must have a lawful basis, be limited to what is needed, and be logged. Common lawful reasons for disclosure include the patient’s consent, direct care, public health duties, court orders and preventing serious harm.

Country rules differ: the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the US Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Privacy Rule and the UK Data Protection Act 2018 are examples. Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 also applies. Always check current national law.

sections.heading: Ethics and dilemmas
sections.text:
Codes require accuracy, confidentiality, competence and honesty. Coding dilemmas arise when pressure to maximise payment conflicts with truthful documentation. The code must reflect the record, not the fee. In research, seek ethics approval, use least data and protect identifiers. In data sharing, use data only for the agreed purpose and share the minimum.

A reasoned approach: state facts, duties and stakeholders, apply autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice, consult ethics committee, choose the least intrusive option, and document it. Case: a coder is asked to add a diagnosis not in the notes. Refuse, query the clinician in writing and record it.

keyPoints: Valid consent is voluntary, informed and specific; capacity is decision-specific and may change.
Minors and deceased patients have special rules that vary by country, so check national law and policy.
Retention periods and disclosure duties are set by law and professional guidance, not by habit.
Disclose only the minimum needed, under a lawful basis, and log the disclosure.
Coding must reflect the documented record, never pressure to increase payment.

For ethical dilemmas, identify duties, apply autonomy (respect choice), beneficence (do good), non-maleficence (avoid harm) and justice (fairness), consult, choose the least intrusive option and document the decision.

en.title: Release of information and patient access
en.short: How patients and third parties obtain records: consent, identity, minimum disclosure and logs.

sections.heading: Access and consent
sections.text: Release of information is the controlled process of giving health record content to a patient or another person. Patient access means the person may inspect or obtain a copy of their own record, subject to law and policy. Valid consent must be informed, specific, voluntary and given by a capable patient or authorised representative. For a child or adult lacking capacity, follow current law. Check identity first, using at least two identifiers.

sections.heading: Disclosure workflow
sections.text: Third-party disclosure needs a lawful basis: usually the patient’s signed consent naming the recipient, purpose, records and time period, or legal authority such as a court order. Verify the requester’s identity and authority, confirm scope, and apply minimum necessary disclosure, meaning release only data needed for that purpose. Remove other people’s information unless consent or law allows it. Record every disclosure. Case: Amina asks for her antenatal record. The clerk checks identity, gives the copy and logs it. Her insurer later asks for the same record. Without Amina’s signed consent naming the insurer, the clerk refuses.

sections.heading: Fees, time limits, exceptions
sections.text: Fees, response time limits and exceptions differ by country and institution, so check current statute, regulator guidance and local policy. Some laws allow a copying fee but not a fee to inspect your own record; others set fixed response periods. Exceptions may allow disclosure without consent for emergency care, statutory reporting, court orders, serious public health risks or safeguarding. Use the least information necessary and document the legal basis. For example, Nigeria’s National Health Act 2014, the UK Data Protection Act 2018 and the US HIPAA Privacy Rule differ.

sections.heading: Disclosure logs
sections.text: A disclosure log records the date, requester, recipient, purpose, legal basis, items released, staff member and any fee. It supports audit, complaint handling and detection of improper access. Keep the log secure and confidential. Train staff to refuse unclear requests politely and refer them to the privacy officer.

keyPoints: Patient access gives a person the right to inspect or copy their own record, subject to law and policy.
Valid consent is informed, specific, voluntary and given by a capable patient or authorised representative.
Verify identity with at least two identifiers before releasing any information.
Third-party disclosure needs a lawful basis, and only the minimum necessary information should be released.
Record every disclosure in a secure log with date, recipient, purpose, legal basis and items released.
Fees, time limits and exceptions vary by country and institution, so check current law and local policy.

en.title: Quality improvement and patient safety
en.short: Quality indicators, clinical audit, incident reporting, PDSA and using health information safely.

sections.heading: Quality and safety
sections.text:
Quality improvement is the planned, repeated effort to make care safer, more effective and more efficient. Patient safety means reducing avoidable harm during care.

A quality indicator is a measurable statement of how well a service meets a standard, such as the proportion of records with a documented allergy. Health information supplies the numbers: registers, records, incident logs and reports. Indicators need a clear numerator, denominator and data source, so staff measure the same thing.

sections.heading: Audit and PDSA
sections.text:
Clinical audit compares current practice with an agreed standard, then changes practice and re-audits. It is not research; it checks whether known good practice is followed. The plan-do-study-act (PDSA) cycle is a small-scale improvement method: Plan a change, Do it on a small scale, Study the result, Act by adopting, adapting or abandoning it.

For example, an audit of 40 records finds 30 with allergy status recorded. Compliance is 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75, or 75 per cent. After a PDSA change to the admission form, a repeat audit of 40 records finds 36, or 90 per cent. The team keeps the change if it is sustained.

sections.heading: Incident reporting
sections.text:
An incident is any event that harmed, or could have harmed, a patient. A near miss is an incident stopped before harm occurred. Incident reporting should be simple, confidential and focused on learning.

A just culture distinguishes human error from reckless behaviour: staff are not blamed for system faults, but deliberate unsafe acts are managed fairly. Reports are reviewed for patterns, such as repeated missing results or equipment failures, and the findings feed improvement.

sections.heading: Accreditation and findings
sections.text:
Accreditation is an external review against published standards, and it depends on evidence from health information: policies, audit reports, incident trends and complete records.

When presenting findings, describe processes and rates, not individuals. Use anonymised examples, show the standard and the gap, and propose a system change. National accreditation rules and patient safety guidance differ by country, so check the current official source.

keyPoints: Quality improvement is planned, repeated change; patient safety is reducing avoidable harm.
A quality indicator needs a clear numerator, denominator and data source.
Clinical audit compares practice with a standard and re-audits after change.
PDSA tests a small change through Plan, Do, Study and Act.
Report incidents and near misses to learn from system faults, not to blame individuals.
Health information provides evidence for accreditation and improvement, and compliance is numerator ÷ denominator × 100.

en.title: Health information management operations and leadership
en.short: Planning, staffing, budgeting, workflow, vendors, projects, change and team leadership in HIM services.

sections.heading: Planning and staffing
sections.text: Department planning sets goals, services and resources for a health information service. It starts with the organisation’s needs and the legal rules that apply in the country, such as health records and data protection laws. Staffing follows workload and skill mix. Skill mix means the right balance of records officers, coders, analysts and supervisors. Plan rotas, cover for leave, induction and continuing training. Retention matters: unclear roles and poor supervision drive staff away.

sections.heading: Budgeting and workflow
sections.text: A budget is a plan for income and spending over a period. Typical lines are personnel, equipment, supplies, training and maintenance. Use realistic prices and check local procurement rules. For example, if a unit needs 1,200 new folders at 250 currency units each, the materials cost is 1,200 × 250 = 300,000. Add a contingency, meaning a reserve for unexpected costs, only if policy allows. Workflow design maps each step from patient arrival to record filing or data entry, removes duplication and tests the design with the people who do the work.

sections.heading: Vendors and projects
sections.text: Vendor management means choosing and overseeing suppliers, such as records storage firms or software companies. Write clear requirements, compare total cost, check data protection and ask for a service level agreement (SLA), which states the service and remedies. Keep an exit plan. Project management controls scope, schedule, budget, risks and stakeholders. A project charter states the goal and who approves changes. Review risks regularly and involve users early.

sections.heading: Leadership and performance
sections.text: Team leadership gives clear roles, fair supervision and safe ways to raise problems. Change management is the structured process of moving people to a new system or workflow. Communicate why, train staff, listen to feedback and allow time. Performance monitoring uses indicators, audits and dashboards to compare actual work with targets, then acts on gaps. Indicators may include record completeness, coding timeliness and data quality. Check current national regulations and professional standards, because they differ by country and change.

keyPoints: Department planning aligns services, staffing and resources with organisational needs and national regulations.
Staffing follows workload and skill mix, with rota cover, induction and continuing training.
A budget lists personnel, equipment, supplies, training and maintenance; check prices and procurement rules.
Workflow design maps steps, removes duplication and is tested with the people who do the work.
Vendor management needs clear requirements, an SLA, data protection checks and an exit plan; project management controls scope, schedule, budget, risks and stakeholders.
Change management supports people through new systems, and performance monitoring uses indicators and audits to compare results with targets.

en.title: Health financing, billing and reimbursement
en.short: Financing models, claims, case mix, fraud risks and country payment rules.

sections.heading: How care is financed
sections.text: Health services are financed by pooled money or direct payment. Tax-funded systems use government revenue. Social health insurance pools contributions from workers and employers, often through a national fund. Private insurance and out-of-pocket payments are common elsewhere. Donor and community schemes also matter. Each model sets incentives: fee-for-service pays for each service given, so it rewards more activity, capitation pays a fixed amount per enrolled person, and budgets limit total spending. Rules differ by country and change, so check the national health financing authority.

sections.heading: Coding and claims
sections.text: Billing depends on records. Clinicians document diagnoses, procedures and services. Coders translate them into standard codes, such as ICD for diagnoses and national procedure codes. A claim is a request for payment sent to an insurer or fund; the payment the provider receives back is called reimbursement. It must match the record. Incomplete or late records cause rejected claims and lost revenue. Good records also support audit and patient safety.

sections.heading: Case mix and payment
sections.text: Case mix describes how complex a provider’s patients are. A case mix index compares the average cost or weight of a provider’s cases with a standard. Case-based payment, such as diagnosis related groups in some countries, pays a fixed amount for a defined patient group. Example: if a hospital’s 1,000 discharges have total relative weights of 1,200, the case mix index is 1,200 ÷ 1,000 = 1.20. If the base payment is 50,000 units, average payment is 1.20 × 50,000 = 60,000 units. This is a generic illustration, not a real tariff.

sections.heading: Fraud and compliance
sections.text: Fraud is intentional deception for gain, such as billing for care not given or changing a code to a higher-paying one (upcoding). Abuse is improper practice that may be unintentional, such as unbundling services that should be one claim. Risks include duplicate claims, false records and phantom patients. Controls include staff training, separation of duties, claim audits and secure data handling. Follow the payment rules of the country where you work; they differ and change, so use current official guidance.

keyPoints: Health financing comes from pooled sources such as taxes, social insurance, private insurance or donor schemes, plus direct out-of-pocket payments, and each model creates different incentives.
A claim is a request for payment and must be supported by accurate, complete and timely clinical records and codes.
Case mix index = total relative weights ÷ number of discharges, and it shows how complex a provider’s patient mix is compared with a standard.
Case-based payment pays a fixed amount for a defined patient group, so coding quality affects both revenue and fairness.
Fraud is intentional deception for gain, such as upcoding, while abuse is improper practice that may be unintentional.
Payment rules differ by country and change, so follow current official guidance and use audits and internal controls.

en.title: Public health informatics and registries
en.short: Population health systems: disease and immunisation registries, GIS, dashboards, sharing and privacy.

sections.heading: Population health systems
sections.text:
Public health informatics is the use of information and computer science to support public health: counting cases, planning services and responding to outbreaks. A population health information system collects and analyses data about groups, not only individual patients. It draws on notifications (official reports of cases to health authorities), laboratories, clinics and registries.

A registry is a systematic list of cases or events that meet defined criteria, kept for a defined population and purpose. Examples are cancer registries, tuberculosis registers and immunisation registries.

sections.heading: Registries, GIS and dashboards
sections.text:
An immunisation registry records vaccinations and can produce coverage figures and reminders. A disease registry follows people with a condition over time. A geographic information system (GIS) links data to places and displays maps, so staff can see where cases cluster.

A public health dashboard presents selected indicators as charts or maps, usually updated regularly. Dashboards help managers see trends, but the underlying data quality must be checked.

sections.heading: Sharing and privacy
sections.text:
Data sharing moves data between facilities, laboratories and public health agencies. It needs agreed standards, unique identifiers and data-sharing agreements.

Privacy safeguards include a legal basis under national data protection and health law, collecting only the minimum data needed, de-identification or aggregation, access controls, audit trails and secure transfer. Rules differ by country, so check the current national law and local policy.

sections.heading: Planning and outbreak response
sections.text:
Planners use registry and dashboard data to estimate need, place services and monitor coverage. In an outbreak, rapid sharing helps confirm cases, map spread and target vaccination.

Case: in a fictional district, the immunisation registry shows low coverage in one ward; a GIS map links this to a measles cluster; the dashboard triggers a vaccination campaign. The lesson is that useful information depends on timely reporting, clear definitions and privacy protection.

keyPoints: Public health informatics uses information systems to support population health, planning and outbreak response.
A registry is a systematic list of cases or events for a defined population and purpose.
Immunisation registries track vaccinations and coverage; disease registries follow cases over time.
GIS links data to places, and dashboards display indicators for monitoring.
Data sharing needs standards, identifiers and agreements; privacy safeguards include legal basis, minimum data, de-identification, access control and audit.
Registry and dashboard data guide planning and outbreak response, but depend on timely, high-quality reporting.

en.title: Research methods in health information
en.short: Framing questions, designs, sampling, data, ethics, analysis and reporting in health information research.

sections.heading: Framing the question
sections.text: A research question states exactly what you will study. It should be focused, answerable and useful. For quantitative work, PICO helps: population, intervention or exposure, comparison and outcome. For qualitative work, PICo uses population, phenomenon of interest and context. Example: In one district hospital, does a computerised reminder improve completeness of antenatal records compared with paper records? A vague question such as how can records be improved is too broad for a small project.

sections.heading: Designs and sampling
sections.text: Quantitative designs measure numbers and test associations, such as surveys or cohort studies. Qualitative designs explore experiences and meanings, using interviews or focus groups. Mixed methods combine both. Sampling is choosing participants. Probability sampling, such as simple random sampling, supports generalisation. Purposive sampling selects information-rich cases. For a proportion, n = Z² p(1−p) / e², where Z is the z-value for your confidence level (1.96 for 95%). If p = 0.5, e = 0.05 and Z = 1.96, n = (1.96² × 0.5 × 0.5) / 0.05² = 384.16, so recruit 385.

sections.heading: Data and ethics
sections.text: Data collection uses questionnaires, record reviews, interviews or observation. Pilot the tool on a few cases, train collectors and define each variable. Data management means storing files safely, using consistent codes and keeping a data dictionary. Ethics approval is needed before you collect data from people or their records. Informed consent explains purpose, risks, benefits and the right to withdraw. Protect confidentiality, minimise data and follow local law and national guidance, which vary.

sections.heading: Analysis and reporting
sections.text: Basic analysis summarises data before testing. Quantitative analysis uses counts, percentages, means and standard deviations, then confidence intervals or suitable tests. Qualitative analysis groups coded text into themes. Critical appraisal asks whether the question, design, sample and analysis fit together, and whether bias or confounding, where a third factor distorts the association, could explain the result. Report using IMRaD: introduction, methods, results and discussion. State limitations and do not claim causation from a weak design.

keyPoints: A good research question is focused, answerable and feasible; PICO suits quantitative questions and PICo suits qualitative ones.
Quantitative designs measure and test; qualitative designs explore meaning; mixed methods combine both.
Probability sampling supports generalisation, while purposive sampling selects information-rich cases.
For a proportion, n = Z² p(1−p) / e²; with p = 0.5, e = 0.05 and Z = 1.96 for 95% confidence, n = 385.
Pilot tools, define variables, keep a data dictionary and obtain ethics approval and informed consent before collecting data from people or their records.
Appraise and report studies by checking question, design, sample, analysis, bias and limitations; use IMRaD.

en.title: Advanced health informatics
en.short: Socio-technical theory, clinical decision support, implementation, evaluation, alert fatigue and equity.

sections.heading: Socio-technical view
sections.text: Health informatics studies how health data are collected, stored, shared and used, and how people, tasks, technology, organisation and wider environment interact. Socio-technical theory says a system succeeds only when these parts fit together; a good app in a poorly designed workflow can still fail. A health information system (HIS) is the people, processes and software used to collect, store, share and use health data. The NASSS framework (Nonadoption, Abandonment, Scale-up, Spread, Sustainability) helps teams judge complexity across condition, technology, value, adopters, organisation, wider system and adaptation over time. Use it before and during implementation, not only after go-live.

sections.heading: Clinical decision support
sections.text: Clinical decision support (CDS) gives clinicians patient-specific information or prompts at the point of care. Examples are allergy warnings, overdue screening reminders and order sets. Good CDS is relevant, evidence-based, timely, unobtrusive and easy to act on. It should tell the user what to do, not only that a problem exists. Governance matters: who approves rules, how often they are reviewed, and how local guidelines are updated. CDS is not a substitute for clinical judgement.

sections.heading: Implementation and evaluation
sections.text: Implementation is planned change, not installing software. Map current workflows, involve users early, train by role, test with real cases, and provide support after go-live. Evaluation asks whether the system is used, safe, effective, efficient, equitable and acceptable. Frameworks such as RE-AIM (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance) and the Quadruple Aim can structure measures. Include baseline data, process measures and patient outcomes; compare before and after, and watch for inequity by language, disability, gender or rural access.

sections.heading: Unintended consequences
