sections.text: Unintended consequences include alert fatigue, where too many warnings make staff ignore important ones; workflow disruption; copy-and-paste errors; and new safety risks. Imagine a district hospital in Ghana where a team adds a sepsis alert for every fever. Nurses Amina and Kwame dismiss it repeatedly, then miss a genuinely unwell patient. Mitigate by limiting alerts to high-value actionable rules, auditing overrides, and redesigning workflow with users. Judge success by safety, equity and real use, not logins.

keyPoints: Socio-technical theory says success depends on fit among people, tasks, technology, organisation and environment.
NASSS helps assess nonadoption, abandonment, scale-up, spread and sustainability.
Good clinical decision support is relevant, evidence-based, timely, actionable and governed.
Implementation is planned workflow change with users, training and post go-live support.
Evaluation should cover use, safety, effectiveness, efficiency, equity and outcomes, with baseline data.
Alert fatigue and workflow disruption are common unintended consequences; limit alerts to high-value actionable rules and audit overrides.

en.title: Health data analytics and predictive modelling
en.short: Preparing, exploring, visualising and modelling health data, with validation, bias and governance.

sections.heading: Preparing data
sections.text:
Data preparation turns raw records into an analysis-ready table. Define the unit of analysis, such as one patient or one admission, choose the outcome and predictors, and check identifiers, dates, units and coding.

Clean impossible values, document changes, and handle missing data explicitly: complete-case analysis is simple but can bias results if missingness is not random. Avoid data leakage, where outcome or future information enters the predictors. Split data before tuning.

sections.heading: Exploring and visualising
sections.text:
Exploratory analysis describes the data before modelling: counts, means or medians, ranges, and plots such as histograms, scatter plots and time series. Visualisation should show uncertainty and group differences without hiding missing values.

An association means two variables vary together; it does not prove causation. Confounding, reverse causation and selection can create associations. A predictive model exploits association, not necessarily a causal mechanism.

sections.heading: Prediction and validation
sections.text:
Predictive modelling estimates an outcome from predictors. Basic machine learning includes logistic regression for binary outcomes, decision trees and random forests. Fit on training data and evaluate on separate test data; cross-validation gives a more stable estimate. Report discrimination and calibration.

For a binary outcome, sensitivity = true positives ÷ (true positives + false negatives), specificity = true negatives ÷ (true negatives + false positives), and positive predictive value = true positives ÷ (true positives + false positives). Example: 80 true positives, 20 false negatives, 90 true negatives, 10 false positives. Sensitivity = 80 ÷ 100 = 0.80; specificity = 90 ÷ 100 = 0.90; PPV = 80 ÷ 90 = 0.89.

sections.heading: Bias and governance
sections.text:
Bias can enter through sampling, measurement, missing data, labels and model choice. Interpretability means explaining how a model reaches predictions; simple models and feature importance help, but explanations can mislead.

Governance covers lawful and ethical use: data protection, consent or other legal basis, access control, audit, versioning and monitoring after deployment. Check performance in subgroups, because overall accuracy may hide failure in a minority group. Use analytics to support, not replace, clinical judgement.

keyPoints: Prepare data by defining the unit of analysis, cleaning values, documenting changes and handling missing data.
Split data before tuning; use a training set and separate test set or cross-validation to reduce optimistic results.
Sensitivity = TP ÷ (TP + FN); specificity = TN ÷ (TN + FP); PPV = TP ÷ (TP + FP).
Association does not prove causation; confounding and selection can create misleading patterns.
Check bias, calibration and subgroup performance, and use interpretable models where decisions affect people.
Governance requires lawful basis, access control, audit and monitoring after deployment.

en.title: Advanced research methods and dissertation
en.short: Design, sampling, instruments, data analysis, ethics, reproducibility, writing and defence for a master’s dissertation.

sections.heading: Design and sampling
sections.text:
Advanced designs answer a question. Quantitative designs include experiments, quasi-experiments and observational studies; they test hypotheses and estimate effects. Qualitative approaches, such as interview studies and case studies, explore meaning. Mixed methods combine both, for example a survey followed by interviews to explain the numbers.

Sampling is choosing participants. Probability sampling, such as random or stratified sampling, supports generalisation. Non-probability sampling, such as purposive or snowball sampling, limits generalisation. State the sampling frame (the list you sample from), inclusion criteria and non-response plan.

sections.heading: Instruments and data
sections.text:
An instrument is the tool used to collect data, such as a questionnaire or interview guide. Develop it from theory and prior studies, then test content validity, reliability and usability in a pilot.

Data management begins before collection: define each variable in a data dictionary, set rules for missing data, and store files securely. Analysis must match the design. Quantitative analysis may use descriptive statistics, confidence intervals and regression. Qualitative analysis may use thematic analysis with a coding trail. Mixed methods need an explicit integration point.

sections.heading: Ethics and reproducibility
sections.text:
Seek approval from the institutional review board or ethics committee before collecting data. Explain informed consent, confidentiality, data protection and risks to vulnerable groups.

Follow national data protection law and local rules, which vary by country. Reproducibility means another researcher can repeat your analysis from your data and documentation and get the same results. Keep a protocol, dated instrument versions, a data dictionary, analysis code and an audit trail. Report unexpected findings. Do not fabricate, falsify or selectively report results.

sections.heading: Writing and defence
sections.text:
Write the dissertation in a clear structure, usually introduction, methods, results and discussion. Use reporting guidelines for your design. Present tables and figures that answer the question.

In the defence, summarise the question, methods, main findings and limitations. Justify your design and sampling choices, show how you managed bias, and explain what the findings do and do not support. A case: a student studying clinic waiting time collects 120 records and interviews 8 staff. She reports the response rate, themes and how the findings agree or differ.

keyPoints: A dissertation design must follow from a precise question, not from convenience.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; purposive and snowball sampling do not.
Instruments need validity, reliability and pilot testing before full data collection.

For a proportion, a simple sample size formula is n = Z² p(1 − p) / e², where Z is the standard normal value for the confidence level, p is the expected proportion and e is the margin of error, before allowing for non-response.
Ethics approval, informed consent and secure data management are required before collection.
Reproducibility needs a protocol, data dictionary, dated instruments, analysis code and audit trail.

en.title: Data governance, AI and ethics in health information
en.short: Secondary use, consent, privacy, security, equity, regulation and AI ethics.

sections.heading: Governance and secondary use
sections.text: Data governance is the rules, roles and controls for how health data are collected, accessed, shared and used. Secondary use means using data for a purpose other than the one they were collected for, such as research, planning or quality improvement. Governance asks who may use data, for what, under what safeguards and for how long. It usually requires a lawful basis, impact assessment, minimisation and de-identification. De-identification lowers risk but does not remove it, because records can sometimes be re-identified.

sections.heading: Consent, privacy, equity
sections.text: Consent is informed agreement. It may be specific or broad, and some countries allow research waivers under strict oversight. Privacy is control over access to one’s information; confidentiality is the duty to keep it; security is technical and organisational protection, such as access control, encryption and audit trails. Equity means fair access to benefits and protection from harm. Secondary use can improve planning but may expose marginalised groups or leave them out if datasets are incomplete. Regulation differs: the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation, the US HIPAA and Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 take different approaches. Check current national law and ethics guidance.

sections.heading: AI ethics and bias
sections.text: AI in health includes prediction, triage and image reading. Bias arises when training data or design reflect past inequities, so a model may work less well for under-represented groups. Transparency means explaining how a model was built, tested and used. Accountability means a named person or body is responsible for decisions and harms. Patient trust depends on consent, clear communication and routes to challenge decisions. A human must remain responsible for clinical decisions.

sections.heading: Accountability and case
sections.text: Case: a Kenyan district hospital shares records with researchers. It should define purpose, obtain ethics approval, remove identifiers, limit access, audit use and report back to the community. If adding an AI triage tool, test it on local data and monitor performance by sex and age. WHO guidance stresses autonomy, safety, equity, transparency and accountability.

keyPoints: Secondary use is use beyond the original purpose; it needs a lawful basis, oversight and de-identification.
Consent may be specific or broad; privacy, confidentiality and security are distinct safeguards.
Equity requires checking who benefits and who is missed or harmed by data use.
AI bias can arise from unrepresentative data and can worsen health inequities.
Transparency and named accountability are needed for patient trust and safe AI.
Data protection law and AI guidance differ by country; check current national and WHO guidance.
